entry.title: Breach Notification Automation Against a Fixed Regulatory Deadline
entry.summary:
Breach Notification Pipeline Against a Fixed Regulatory Deadline
Breach notification is a race against a statutory clock, not a writing task. Singapore PDPA guidance and GDPR Article 33 converge on the same constraint: assessment and regulator notification inside a fixed window. Automation wins that race only when the pipeline is built before the incident, because the clock starts at discovery, not at the first meeting. A notification pipeline that depends on human kickoff loses the first hours to coordination. Triage calls, spreadsheet trackers, and legal review queues consume the window that regulators measure. The pipeline must start from a machine event: a detection alert that opens a timestamped case record with the deadline computed and written into the case row itself. The archite…

entry.summary:
Short answer: to split a video with FFmpeg, use the segment muxer: ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -map 0 -c copy -f segment -segment_times 4.041667,7.083333 -reset_timestamps 1 part_%03d.mp4
That is lossless and fast, but with -c copy FFmpeg can only cut on keyframes, so -segment_time 2 does not mean "2-second parts". entry.title: Cheap, Simple Webhook Task Processing for Node.js SaaS
entry.summary: Short answer: for a Node.js SaaS that sends a weekly digest to active logistics customers, start with a durable queue, an explicit rate limiter, idempotent delivery records, and bounded exponential backoff; choose the cheapest simple option only after it can prove those delivery guarantees. I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. The failure pattern is predictable: a timer fires, a webhook is sent, the process dies before recording the result, and the next retry sends the same business event again. The opposite failure is just as bad. A retry loop ignores the receiver's rate limit, turns a small outage into a queue storm, and delays every customer's digest.
